question.problem:
Consider the boundary value problem

$$
{y}^{″}-12\lambda {y}^{′}+36{\lambda }^{2}y=0,\,{y}^{′}(1)=0,\,y(2)+6{y}^{′}(2)=0,\,1\le x\le 2,\,\lambda \in R.
$$

Find the eigenvalues and eigenfunctions of this problem. Assume that $B$ and $C$ are constants.

$\,$ The eigenvalues are $\lambda =$ {{field-1}}.

$\,$ The eigenfunctions are $y=$ {{field-2}}.
question.worked_solution:
We consider the cases $\lambda =0$ and $\lambda \ne 0$ separately, since they correspond to different solutions.

**Case 1**: First, we consider $\lambda =0.$

Setting $\lambda =0$ gives the equation

$$
{y}^{″}=0.
$$

Integrating this equation gives

$$
y=Ax+B.
$$

Applying the conditions ${y}^{′}(1)=0$ and $y(2)+6{y}^{′}(2)=0$ yields the trivial solution $y≡0.$ Since the zero solution is not an eigenfunction, $\lambda =0$ is not an eigenvalue.

**Case 2**: Next, we consider $\lambda \ne 0.$

To find the fundamental solutions, we set $y={e}^{mx}.$ The auxiliary equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}{m}^{2}-12\lambda m+36{\lambda }^{2} & =0 \\ (m-6\lambda )(m-6\lambda ) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the double root $m=6\lambda .$ So, the fundamental solutions are

$$
{y}_{1}(x)={e}^{6\lambda x},\,{y}_{2}(x)=x{e}^{6\lambda x}
$$

and the general solution is

$$
y=A{e}^{6\lambda x}+Bx{e}^{6\lambda x}.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =6A\lambda {e}^{6\lambda x}+B{e}^{6\lambda x}+6B\lambda x{e}^{6\lambda x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the boundary condition ${y}^{′}(1)=0$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}6A\lambda {e}^{6\lambda }+B{e}^{6\lambda }+6B\lambda {e}^{6\lambda } & =0 \\ 6A\lambda +B+6B\lambda  & =0 \\ (6\lambda )A+(1+6\lambda )B & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the boundary condition $y(2)+6{y}^{′}(2)=0$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}A{e}^{12\lambda }+2B{e}^{12\lambda }+6(6A\lambda {e}^{12\lambda }+B{e}^{12\lambda }+12B\lambda {e}^{12\lambda }) & =0 \\ A+2B+6(6A\lambda +B+12B\lambda ) & =0 \\ A+2B+36A\lambda +6B+72B\lambda  & =0 \\ (1+36\lambda )A+(8+72\lambda )B & =0 \\ (1+36\lambda )A+8(1+9\lambda )B & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the following systems of equations for $A$ and $B:$

$$
\{\begin{aligned}(6\lambda )A+(1+6\lambda )B=0 \\ (1+36\lambda )A+(8+72\lambda )B=0\end{aligned}
$$

This homogeneous linear system has a nontrivial solution if and only if the determinant is zero. This gives

$$
|\begin{aligned}6\lambda  & 1+6\lambda  \\ 1+36\lambda  & 8+72\lambda \end{aligned}|=0.
$$

So, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}6\lambda (8+72\lambda )-(1+6\lambda )(1+36\lambda ) & =0 \\ 48\lambda +432{\lambda }^{2}-(1+42\lambda +216{\lambda }^{2}) & =0 \\ 216{\lambda }^{2}+6\lambda -1 & =0 \\ (12\lambda +1)(18\lambda -1) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we have the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=-\frac{1}{12}\text{ and }{\lambda }_{2}=\frac{1}{18}.$

Finally, we find the eigenfunction corresponding to each eigenvalue:

- Consider ${\lambda }_{1}=-\frac{1}{12}.$ Then, we have the solution

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{1}(x) & =A{e}^{6{\lambda }_{1}x}+Bx{e}^{6{\lambda }_{1}x} \\  & =A{e}^{-x/2}+Bx{e}^{-x/2}\end{aligned}
$$

and substituting ${\lambda }_{1}$ into

$$
(6\lambda )A+(1+6\lambda )B=0
$$

we get

$$
-\frac{1}{2}A+\frac{1}{2}B=0
$$

which gives $A=B,$ where $B$ is a free parameter. Thus, the eigenfunction corresponding to this eigenvalue is

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{1}(x) & =B{e}^{-x/2}+Bx{e}^{-x/2} \\  & =B{e}^{-x/2}(x+1).\end{aligned}
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=\frac{1}{18},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{2}(x) & =A{e}^{6{\lambda }_{2}x}+Bx{e}^{6{\lambda }_{2}x} \\  & =A{e}^{x/3}+Bx{e}^{x/3}\end{aligned}
$$

and substituting ${\lambda }_{2}$ into

$$
(6\lambda )A+(1+6\lambda )B=0
$$

we get

$$
\frac{1}{3}A+\frac{4}{3}B=0\,⇒\,A=-4B
$$

where $B$ is a free parameter. Thus, the eigenfunction corresponding to this eigenvalue is

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{2}(x) & =-4B{e}^{x/3}+Bx{e}^{x/3} \\  & =B{e}^{x/3}(x-4) \\  & =C{e}^{x/3}(x-4)\end{aligned}
$$

where we have set $C=B.$

So, the eigenfunctions corresponding to ${\lambda }_{1}$ and ${\lambda }_{2},$ respectively, are $B{e}^{-x/2}(x+1)\text{ and }C{e}^{x/3}(x-4).$
